source.version: arXiv 2411.03827v1 of 2024-11-06 (PDF on file, read page by page); not the CUI 2025 version of record (doi 10.1145/3719160.3736633)
source.title_on_document: DesignMinds: Enhancing Video-Based Design Ideation with Vision-Language Model and Context-Injected Large Language Model

supplement.where: Supplementary Text 1 and 2, p. 23 of the PDF
supplement.holds: Task instructions shown to participants (Text 1) and the raters' scoring criteria for fluency, flexibility, and originality (Text 2); no extra statistics

paper_design_summary: Thirty-five design students at the authors' university were randomly divided into an experimental group (N=18) that used DesignMinds, a chatbot combining a vision-language model with GPT-4 and a design-book knowledge base, and a control group (N=17) that ideated without the chatbot. Each participant watched two short videos (cooking, construction; order counterbalanced) and wrote as many improvement ideas as possible in 15 minutes per video. Three independent raters scored the ideas for fluency, flexibility, and originality; the paper also reports eye-tracking and UX/technology-acceptance questionnaires.

studies.label: Lab experiment: video-based design ideation with or without DesignMinds

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to the DesignMinds chatbot (experimental group) versus the same interface with the chatbot hidden (control group)
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly divided into two groups: the experimental group, which interacted with the chatbot DesignMinds, and the control group, where participants continued their usual practice for design inspiration.
assignment.locator: p. 9, Fig. 4 caption; also p. 5, Section 4 (between-subject study design)

arms.name: Experimental group
arms.description: Watched each video and ideated with the DesignMinds chatbot (VLM + GPT-4 with design-book RAG) beside a note-taking space

arms.name: Control group
arms.description: Same videos and note-taking space with the chatbot hidden; ideated as they normally would

participants.who: Design graduates from the authors' design faculty: university students (BSc and MSc) or PhD candidates; 17 female, 18 male; mean age 25.4. Group sizes N=18 and N=17 are from Fig. 4; no exclusions are reported, and the t-tests on the idea ratings have 33 degrees of freedom, consistent with all 35 analyzed.
participants.quote: We enlisted 35 design graduates (17 females and 18 males) from the design faculty at our university
participants.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; group sizes p. 9, Fig. 4; t(33) p. 11, Section 5.1

ai_tool.name_model: DesignMinds: blip2-opt-6.7b vision-language model plus GPT-4 API (gpt-4-0125-preview) with RAG over six design books (text-embedding-ada-002, LlamaIndex), Gradio front end
ai_tool.how_used: Participants watched the video, chatted freely with the chatbot about the video content and improvements, and wrote their ideas in a note-taking space (pp. 4-6, 10)

task.description: Watch two Ego4D videos (cooking and construction, about 3 minutes each, order counterbalanced) and write as many ideas as possible for improving the processes shown

contrasts.reported: Experimental 4.74 ± 1.018 points vs control 3.35 ± 0.583 points (7-point Likert, average of three raters); independent t-test t(33) = 4.674, p < .001

outcomes.name: Flexibility of ideas (number of domains and subdomains covered)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Experimental 7.17 ± 3.511 points vs control 5.12 ± 1.074 points; independent t-test t(33) = 2.304, p = .014
No significant difference: independent t-test t(33) = 1.885, p = .068; arm means shown only in the Fig. 5 radar chart

eligibility.reason: Randomized between-subject lab experiment (p. 9, Fig. 4) with 35 participants in total (18 DesignMinds, 17 control; p. 8 Section 4.1 and p. 9 Fig. 4), well below the 50-person threshold. Listed in the screening report as a small randomized experiment; left out of the dataset.

one_line_finding: With the DesignMinds chatbot, 18 design students' ideas scored higher than 17 controls' on originality (4.74 vs 3.35, t(33) = 4.674, p < .001) and flexibility (7.17 vs 5.12, t(33) = 2.304, p = .014), with no significant fluency difference (t(33) = 1.885, p = .068) (p. 11, Section 5.1).
